opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that today, building a custom agent is still very much an artisanal process. You have an engineer, or a small team, who sits down, figures out the task, writes a bunch of prompts, picks a model, wires up some tools, builds a little eval set by hand, and then iterates, tweaking the prompt, swapping models, adding a retrieval step, until it's good enough. That loop takes weeks, sometimes months, and most of it is fairly mechanical once you step back.

So the vision is to treat building the agent itself as a search and optimization problem that another system can run. The user describes what they want in natural language, maybe gives a handful of examples or points to some data, and then a meta-agent takes over. It proposes an architecture: is this a single call, a pipeline, something with tools, something with a planner? It generates synthetic training and evaluation data, because data is almost always the bottleneck. It defines metrics, ideally with the user's input, since "good" is often subjective. And then it runs the optimization loop: tuning prompts, choosing between models, possibly distilling or fine-tuning a smaller model when that makes sense for cost and latency.

A big part of this is having the right abstractions underneath. If your agent is just a giant hand-written prompt string, there's not much for an automated system to grab onto. But if you express it as composable modules with clear inputs and outputs, the way frameworks like DSPy encourage, you have a program the optimizer can actually reason about and improve. That's what makes automation tractable.

The other piece I care about is keeping the human in the loop at the right points. You don't want a black box that disappears and comes back with something. You want the system to surface its decisions, show where it's failing, and ask for feedback on ambiguous cases, because that feedback is incredibly high signal. Ultimately the goal is that a domain expert who isn't an ML engineer can go from an idea to a reliable, deployed agent in hours instead of months. That's when you start seeing agents built for the long tail of tasks that today simply aren't worth the engineering effort.

r001.rationale: It proposes a meta-agent that takes over designing and optimizing the custom agent from the user's description.

r002.rationale: It describes encoding agent development as composable modules with clear inputs and outputs, then having an optimizer reason about and improve them through a defined development loop.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. So the way I think about it is that today, if you want a custom agent that actually works in your domain, you end up with a very manual, very bespoke process. You write prompts, you try a model, you look at outputs, you tweak the prompt, you add a few-shot example, you maybe collect some data and fine-tune, you build evals, and then the model changes under you and you do it all again. That loop is where most of the engineering time goes, and almost none of it is specific to the problem you actually care about.

What we want to do is make that loop itself the thing that gets automated. The user shouldn't have to be a prompt engineer or an ML engineer. They should describe the task, point us at whatever data or examples they have, and tell us what good looks like. From there, the system should do the rest: figure out the right decomposition of the task, generate and refine prompts, choose or train the right model for each piece, build the evaluation harness, and keep iterating against it.

A lot of this comes from what I saw at Google. Recommendation systems went through this exact transition, from hand-tuned heuristics to end-to-end learned systems where the humans specify the objective and the data, and the optimization does the work. I think agents are going to follow the same arc. Right now we're in the hand-tuned phase.

There are a few pieces that matter for making that real. One is that the specification has to be something a domain expert can actually give you. Natural language plus examples, not a config file with forty knobs. Two is that evaluation has to be a first-class artifact, because without a reliable signal you can't automate anything. We spend a lot of effort turning fuzzy human judgment into something measurable, including using models as judges and calibrating them against humans. And three is that small, specialized models often beat a giant general model once you have the data and the eval in place. They're cheaper, faster, more controllable, and you can keep improving them.

So the vision is: you describe your agent, we build and tune it, and it keeps getting better as you use it, without your team having to sit in that loop by hand.

r001.rationale: The response proposes an automated system that builds and tunes custom agents, but does not clearly say that an AI agent is used to build them.

r002.rationale: It describes automating a concrete development loop: decomposing tasks, generating and refining prompts, selecting or training models, building evaluations, and iterating against them.

astra-6.text:
I think the starting point is letting people describe the task they want done, rather than asking them to design an agent. What should it accomplish? What tools can it use? What does a successful result look like? From that, a system could propose a workflow, connect the tools, and build an initial version.

But the important part is closing the loop. Building that first version is only part of the work. You need to run it on representative tasks, evaluate where it fails, and use those failures to improve it. That might mean changing the instructions, giving it better context, or simplifying the workflow.

So I envision an iterative process where the system handles more of the implementation and experimentation, while the person provides the intent and feedback. The person can say, “This is what I wanted, and here’s why this result isn’t quite right,” without having to understand all the machinery underneath.

r001.rationale: It describes a system that takes a person’s task goals and builds an initial agent workflow, then improves it through evaluation and feedback.

r002.rationale: It describes an iterative development process, but does not identify codifying well-defined procedures as a way to automate that work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the opportunity is to move from specifying every step of an agent’s workflow to describing what you want it to accomplish. You provide the task, the tools it can use, and examples of what a good outcome looks like. Then the system can propose an agent, test it, and improve it based on those results.

The evaluation piece is really important. Generating an initial agent is one thing; knowing whether it works reliably is another. You need a feedback loop that helps you understand where it fails and whether a change actually makes it better.

So I envision the developer’s role shifting toward defining the problem, setting constraints, and judging outcomes, while more of the implementation and experimentation becomes automated.

r001.rationale: The response says a system can propose, test, and improve an agent, but does not clearly identify that system as an AI agent building custom AI agents.

r002.rationale: It describes providing tasks, tools, examples, and feedback, but does not identify codifying well-defined agent-development procedures as the automation method.
